title: Operational due diligence: Don’t let your operations undermine the investment case
summary: Discover why operational due diligence matters for emerging hedge fund managers, from risk controls and governance to investor scrutiny and readiness.
body_markdown:
*“You can change the portfolio overnight, but you can’t change the business overnight.”*


For emerging investment managers, much of the early focus when building a fund naturally falls on the investment proposition: creating a differentiated strategy, establishing a track record and convincing investors to allocate.


But winning the investment case is only part of winning an allocation.


Operational due diligence (ODD) looks beyond the strategy to the business supporting it – from its controls, systems and people to its governance, infrastructure and service providers. And for institutional investors, it can be a significant part of the allocation decision.


## Institutionalization is happening earlier


The need to build robust operational foundations earlier is reflected in the latest[AIMA and Marex Emerging Manager Survey](https://www.marex.com/news/2026/06/emerging-manager-survey-2026-hedge-funds) : 86% of investors surveyed cited operational due diligence as the biggest barrier to allocation, underlining just how important operational readiness can be to the fundraising process.


Managers appear to be responding. The research found that emerging managers are investing earlier in infrastructure and in-house capabilities, and at the same time, investors are becoming more willing to consider managers earlier in their lifecycle.


So, what does it take to build a business that is ready for institutional scrutiny?


## Build the operational foundations early


A robust operating model does not necessarily mean replicating the infrastructure of a large, established institution from day one. It means putting in place controls, systems and processes that are appropriate for the size, complexity and strategy of the business.


Cash management is one important area. Managers need clear processes governing how money moves through the business, who can authorize transactions and what checks and approvals are required for movements of client capital in their funds. Appropriate segregation of duties and multiple signatories can help ensure that too much control does not sit with one individual.


The same principle applies to risk management.


Having risk limits documented is one thing; establishing what happens when one is breached is another. If a drawdown limit is reached, for example, who is alerted? Who has the authority to act? Is there sufficient independent oversight outside the investment team, and can someone other than the CIO intervene if necessary? This also ties back to having robust contingency plans for key person risk, especially in a single PM model.


Managers should also consider IT and information security, portfolio and order management systems, risk analytics and document security. People and reporting lines matter too: responsibilities should be clearly defined, controls need sufficient independence and the overall structure should support effective governance.


Finally, counterparties and service providers need to be appropriate for the strategy. The quality and credibility of administrators, auditors, prime brokers and other providers can all form part of an investor’s assessment.


## Outsource the function, not the responsibility


For emerging managers, outsourcing can be an effective way to access specialist expertise and infrastructure without having to build every capability internally.


Compliance and middle- and back-office functions are among those that may be outsourced to external providers. But handing a function to a third party does not remove the manager’s responsibility for understanding and overseeing it.


Managers need to know what their providers are doing, how processes work and how issues are identified and resolved. That can include understanding how records are reconciled between administrators and prime brokers, how breaks are investigated and, where relevant, how less-liquid assets are valued and the degree of independence within that process.


The underlying principle is straightforward: *outsource where it makes sense, but retain visibility and control.*


## What should you expect from the ODD process?


The precise scope of ODD will vary by investor and manager, but a useful way to think about the process is ‘trust and verify’.


Investors are not simply looking for a collection of policies. They want confidence that those policies translate into effective day-to-day controls and that the business operates as the manager says it does.


An investor may begin with a questionnaire or checklist covering the firm’s operational set-up, followed by a more detailed meeting in which the manager walks through its processes and controls.


From there, the focus can move from description to evidence.


If a policy states that a particular process is carried out regularly, an ODD team may ask to see examples from specific dates. If a manager describes a cash-management process, they may be asked to explain how a transaction is executed and who is involved at each stage.


Investors may also independently verify information with administrators, prime brokers and other counterparties, using external information to corroborate what the manager has provided.


This is why relatively basic weaknesses can become significant: insufficient separation between personal and business technology, inadequate controls around cash movements, unclear reporting lines or processes that can be easily circumvented can all raise concerns.


The process can therefore feel closer to an audit than an investment pitch. The emphasis is less on presenting a compelling narrative and more on demonstrating that the business operates as described.


That does not mean every weakness automatically prevents an investment. ODD teams may identify areas for improvement and agree remediation actions that can subsequently be reviewed. But significant deficiencies – or a gap between what a manager says happens and what can actually be demonstrated – can become a much more serious concern.


## Be ready to demonstrate, not just describe


Preparation for ODD should begin well before an investor asks for it.


Keep Due Diligence Questionnaire’s (DDQ), policies and supporting documentation current and readily available. Make sure the people responsible for key processes understand them and can explain how they operate. Know what evidence exists to demonstrate that controls are working, and be prepared to explain how outsourced functions are monitored.


Above all, documentation needs to reflect reality. If you state that a particular process or control is in place, be prepared to demonstrate it. It is better to be clear about what the business currently does than to describe a more sophisticated process that cannot withstand scrutiny.


By the time an investor reaches ODD, you have already done much of the difficult work: building the strategy, establishing the business, developing investor relationships and convincing somebody that the investment proposition merits serious consideration.


Don’t allow avoidable operational weaknesses to undo that work.


Which brings us back to the principle we started with: *you can change the portfolio overnight, but you can’t change the business overnight.*


Building the right operational foundations from the outset often creates a stronger business, makes future growth easier to manage and means that, when an investor is ready to allocate, the infrastructure supporting the strategy is ready too.
